readerQuestion: How can I find the cheapest continuous two-hour electricity window in Home Assistant, check that it matches my tariff, and preview a plan before controlling an appliance?
directAnswer: Match the source to the household tariff, then compare complete contiguous intervals over the allowed operating window. The built-in Nord Pool example previews tomorrow's lowest average two-hour spot-price block between 08:00 and 22:00 in a dated in-app notification. It excludes changing retail charges and appliance load-profile optimization; verify the result before considering supported appliance controls.
originalContribution: Section 2 works through 4/30/5/6-cent prices to show why two cheapest isolated hours differ from the best continuous block. Section 4 supplies an original notification-only planner that validates full allowed-window coverage, compares elapsed durations, converts EUR/MWh once and replaces stale plans before fetching. Section 5 gives concrete harmless verification, including an impossible 25-hour run. The troubleshooting table distinguishes data, time-zone, scaling, tariff and control issues.
limitations: Documentation research and 18 offline Jinja/YAML checks with synthetic fixtures only. No live Home Assistant, Nord Pool account, appliance or savings measurements. The script targets built-in Nord Pool, EUR/MWh responses, 15-minute/hourly slots and a suitable European spot tariff. Time-varying retail charges, solar export, batteries, demand charges and actual appliance load shapes need a different cost model. The example does not control appliances, cache outage plans, retry automatically or replay a missed daily trigger. AI-generated editorial kitchen illustration is not a product test or installation photograph.
proofreadFixes: Automated grandma-proofread PASS after corrections: changed the tax example from saying every candidate cost changes equally to the precise statement that uniform positive adjustments preserve ordering; changed the no-plan message so an oversized requested duration is not misdiagnosed solely as missing data; made the research note explicitly distinguish offline synthetic checks from live Home Assistant and appliance testing. Verified that response_variable is at action level, the config entry is not an entity ID, source prices are per MWh, negative rates are retained, complete-window gaps and overlaps reject the plan, and the initial notification prevents an old result surviving a failed fetch. Confirmed no smart-plug restart assumption, no phone-push claim, no automatic catch-up claim, local/UTC distinction and date-stamped output. Restored unrelated whitespace changes made by the mandatory layout synchronizer; existing articles remain byte-identical to HEAD. Initial desktop capture preceded image decoding; repeated after decode and visually confirmed the cover. All 877 local references and seven primary source URLs passed.

claimChecks.claim: Nord Pool provides market prices rather than complete retail tariffs; its price source needs internet access. Existing sensors and the date-specific action have different scopes and units.

nordpool.get_prices_for_date takes a configuration entry, date, area and currency; each area returns UTC start/end intervals and prices per MWh. The script converts to EUR/kWh once and uses tomorrow only after data is published.
An action response is stored using response_variable at the action level for later steps; the planner uses that response rather than assuming sensor attributes contain tomorrow's full price list.
Script steps stop on error by default. Placing an invalidating notification before the price request prevents a previously successful plan remaining displayed as a fresh result if fetching fails.

Template loops need a namespace to retain accumulated values. The original algorithm was checked offline for complete and missing coverage, negative prices, interval ordering, ties, unsupported periods and mixed hourly/quarter-hour weights.

Timestamps represent actual instants; local time is applied for display. The example calculates tomorrow's local allowed window and compares elapsed seconds, without a fixed UTC offset or 24-row day assumption.
A repeated persistent notification ID replaces the previous frontend notification. It is an in-app message, not a phone push, and the script contains no appliance-control actions.
